sections.heading: Outlets, Breakers and Lights That Act Up
body: A warm plate, a buzzing switch or a light that flickers is a loose or failing connection until someone proves otherwise. A loose connection heats up, and that's how a small problem becomes a fire risk.

items.title: A warm or discolored outlet
items.text: Stop using it and call. Heat at the plate means a connection is loose or failing.

items.title: A breaker that keeps tripping
items.text: It's telling you a circuit is overloaded or has a fault. Resetting it again and again doesn't fix that.

items.title: Lights that flicker
items.text: One fixture flickering is often the bulb. Flicker in several rooms, or when a big appliance starts, points to a loose connection or an overloaded circuit.

items.title: Outlets that work, then don't
items.text: Usually a worn outlet or a loose wire behind it. It tends to get worse, not better.

sections.heading: What Happens When You Call About an Outlet

image.alt: Electrician testing a wall outlet with a meter

body: Tell us what the outlet is doing and which room it's in. We come look at it in person, find the cause and explain what we found in plain words.
Then you decide what gets fixed. A free estimate comes first.

sections.heading: What a Bad Outlet Is Telling You
body: Outlets wear out. Plugs get pulled in and out for years, and the metal inside stops gripping. Most of what goes wrong is one of a short list of things.

items.title: The plate is warm or discolored
items.text: A loose connection makes heat, and heat is how outlets fail badly. Stop using it and call.

items.title: It buzzes, crackles or smells like burning
items.text: That's arcing, and it needs attention now. Unplug what you can, switch off the breaker if you know which one it is, and call.

items.title: It's dead
items.text: Often a tripped breaker or a tripped GFCI somewhere else. If the reset doesn't bring it back, a wire behind the outlet has likely come loose.

items.title: Plugs fall out
items.text: The contacts inside have worn. It's a simple repair, and worth doing before the next cord pulls loose.

items.title: It works, then it doesn't
items.text: An on-again, off-again outlet is a loose connection. It tends to get worse, and a loose connection is the kind that heats.

items.title: It only takes two prongs
items.text: An older outlet with no ground hole can't properly protect a modern plug. Grounding circuits is part of what we do.

sections.quote: If you need any electrical work done you have to call them. Very professional and clean work in a timely manner, with very fair prices.

sections.heading: Replacing a Worn Outlet

image.alt: A dimmer switch and wall plate on a living room wall

body: Most bad outlets are fixed by replacing the outlet itself, not by rewiring the room. A new one grips plugs again and carries its load without heating up.
If the trouble is in the wiring behind it, the repair is bigger. We tell you so before you choose.
Switches, dimmers and fixtures wear the same way, and we repair them too.

sections.heading: When You Need More Outlets
body: Power strips on power strips and cords running across a room are a sign. The room doesn't have enough outlets, or the ones it has are in the wrong place.
Adding outlets is a job we do, on a circuit that can carry the load.

sections.heading: Outlets Near Water
body: Outlets in kitchens, bathrooms, garages and outdoors are usually GFCI protected. A GFCI cuts the power fast when current goes where it shouldn't.
One that trips over and over, or won't reset, is either doing its job or has failed. Either way it's worth a look.

sections.heading: Outlets in Older Homes
body: Older houses were wired when a room needed a lamp and a radio. Now it's a TV, a game console, chargers and a space heater, all on circuits sized for less.
A warm outlet in an older room is often carrying more than the circuit was built for.

sections.heading: Before You Call
body: If you can do it safely, unplug what's on the outlet and look for a tripped breaker. Check the GFCI buttons on outlets in the kitchen, bath, garage or outside, and press reset.
If the outlet is warm, scorched or smells like burning, stop using it. If you see smoke or flames, leave the house and call 911.

items.q: Does it cost anything to call?
items.a: No. Call (316) 262-1440 and describe what the outlet is doing, or ask for a free estimate.

items.q: Is a warm outlet an emergency?
items.a: Treat it as urgent. A warm outlet means a loose or failing connection. Stop using it, and call us. If there's smoke, a burning smell or scorch marks, get out and call 911.

items.q: Do you replace switches and dimmers too?
items.a: Yes. Switch, outlet and fixture repairs are part of the work, and a worn dimmer is a common one.
Yes. Tell us where you'd like them, and we'll tell you what the circuit can handle.

items.q: What if only one outlet in the room is dead?
items.a: Check the breaker and any GFCI first. One dead outlet in a room that otherwise works often has a loose wire behind it. Call, and we'll look.

items.q: Do you work on rentals and businesses?
items.a: Yes. We do commercial work as well as residential.

sections.heading: What Happens When You Call About a Charger

image.alt: Electrical panel with breakers and labeled circuits

body: Tell us the car, the charger you have or want, and where it parks. We come to the house, look at the garage and the panel, and tell you what the install involves.
Then you decide. A free estimate comes first, and nothing gets started until you say so.

sections.heading: What a Charger Install Needs
body: A plug-in charger on a regular outlet adds range slowly. Most people who own an electric car want a faster one, and a faster one asks more of your house.

items.title: A circuit of its own
items.text: A faster home charger usually runs on a dedicated 240-volt circuit. It shouldn't share a breaker with anything else.

items.title: A panel with room
items.text: Your panel has to have space and capacity for the new circuit. In an older house, or one already running AC and other big loads, that's the first thing to check.

items.title: A run from the panel to the garage
items.text: The wire has to get from the panel to the charger. The shorter and more direct the route, the simpler the job.

items.title: A good spot on the wall
items.text: The cable has to reach the car's charging port, and the charger has to be where you can use it and where it's protected from the weather.

items.title: The right size for the car
items.text: Your car can only accept so much power. A bigger charger doesn't charge it faster than the car allows, so check the manual before you buy.

sections.heading: Is Your Panel Ready?
body: A charger is a big, steady load. If the panel is full, old or already near what it can carry, it may need work before a charger goes in.
Panel replacements are part of what we do. We look at the panel in person and tell you what it needs, before you spend anything on the charger.

sections.heading: Outdoors or in the Garage
body: A charger can go inside the garage or on an outside wall. One mounted outside has to be made for weather, and the wiring to it has to be protected too.
We look at where the car parks and tell you what makes sense for that spot.

sections.heading: Planning for a Second Car
body: If a second electric car is likely, say so when you call. Sizing the panel and the run for two chargers now is easier than opening the wall twice.

sections.heading: Before You Buy a Charger
body: Check your car's manual for the most power it accepts at home. Note where the car parks and how close that is to the panel.
Tell us the charger you're looking at when you call. We'll tell you what the install would involve at your house.

items.a: It depends on the panel and what else it's running. We look at it in person and tell you. Panel replacement is part of the work we do.
Depending on the job, a permit and an inspection may be part of a charger install. Ask when you call, and we'll tell you what yours involves.

items.a: Tell us the make and model when you call. We'll look at your garage and panel and tell you what it takes.
Either can work. A charger mounted outside has to be made for weather. We'll look at where the car parks and say what makes sense.

items.a: The wire has to cross the yard, usually through a trench. We do electrical trenching, so it can be part of the same job.
